executive_summary: The dominant thread running through today's content is the consolidation and stress-testing of right-wing political power in America, and whether its ideological foundations hold under scrutiny. The breaking news places Trump's influence directly on trial in six state primaries, with his endorsement of Ken Paxton serving as a concrete measure of his command over the Republican Party machinery. The Atlantic's long-form analysis extends this picture further, arguing that masculinism — the ideological engine increasingly powering the American right — is not a genuine response to male grievance but a coordinated misogynist project, which means the movement's cohesion rests on a reactionary cultural identity rather than a policy agenda. Foreign Affairs reinforces the international dimension of this dynamic, examining how Orbán's model of illiberal nationalism is being re-evaluated as European political confidence reasserts itself. Together, these signals point to a single critical question: whether the right's current ideological and electoral coalition is a durable governing force or a moment of peak consolidation before structural fracture.

newsletters.title: The Evening: I.R.S. to drop Trump audits

items.headline: The I.R.S. will drop its audits of Trump and his family
items.blurb: The Justice Department revealed today that President Trump, his family and his businesses will be shielded from being investigated or prosecuted over their taxes. The provision was signed by acting Attorney General Todd Blanche and quietly posted on the department's website. It's part of an extraordinary new agreement the president struck with his own administration to settle his lawsuit against the I.R.S., where officials had mapped out a plan to fight Trump's claims. Protection from audit could be quite beneficial for Trump. In 2024, my colleagues found that a loss in an I.R.S. audit could cost him more than $100 million. Also part of the deal is a $1.8 billion compensation fund for people who claim to have been the target of politically motivated prosecutions. That fund has been loudly criticized by Democrats as a way to funnel taxpayer money to Trump's allies. Some Republicans in Congress also voiced concerns. John Thune, the Senate majority leader, rarely publicly criticizes Trump but said he "was not a big fan" of the fund.

items.headline: The president aims to reshape his party through primaries
items.blurb: Trump announced today that he was endorsing Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general, a week before his Senate primary against the state's longtime Republican senator, John Cornyn. Many Republicans in Washington see Paxton as the weaker candidate in a general election, given his history of indictment, impeachment and accusations of marital infidelity. But the president praised Paxton for being "extremely loyal" to him, indicating yet again that he was seeking to oust Republican dissenters. That effort is perhaps best exemplified by a big House primary today in Kentucky. There, Thomas Massie, a House Republican who has proved more willing to break with the president than any of his colleagues, is being challenged by Trump's handpicked candidate. It's become the most expensive House primary in years. Trump's influence will also be tested today in Georgia's governor's race, where his preferred candidate is going up against a billionaire health care executive.

items.headline: Ebola cases rise sharply in central Africa
items.blurb: Health officials warned today that an Ebola outbreak in central Africa could last for months. More than 130 people are suspected to have died so far, though experts worry that contact-tracing challenges have led to an undercounting of cases. "I'm deeply concerned about the scale and speed of the epidemic," one W.H.O. official said. The outbreak is centered in the east of the Democratic Republic of Congo, where an ongoing conflict has slowed the public health response. American officials said this week that the U.S. was restricting entry into the country for some travelers.

items.headline: Wemby's World: Did the Spurs star really just do that to OKC?
items.blurb: Forty-eight minutes and 42 seconds. Forty-one points. Twenty-four rebounds. Three assists. Three blocks. One massive 28-foot 3-pointer. That was Victor Wembanyama's stat line from the Spurs' 122-115 double-overtime victory in Game 1 of the Western Conference finals last night. Since blocked shots started being recorded in the 1973-74 season, only three players have put up 40 points, 24 boards and three blocks in a playoff game. Hakeem Olajuwon did it twice in 1987 and 1988. Shaquille O'Neal did it in 2000. Now Wemby.

items.headline: Heartbreak in CT, Clark in L.A.
items.blurb: I was in Connecticut for the Las Vegas Aces' two-game series against the Sun when the WNBA and NBA board of governors' approved the sale of the Sun and their relocation from the Mohegan Tribe to Tilman J. Fertitta in a unanimous vote. Fertitta, who also owns the Houston Rockets, purchased the franchise for a record-breaking $300 million. The Sun will be rebranded as the Comets, the WNBA's original dynasty team, which folded in 2008. Being in Uncasville, Conn., when this news broke, I can tell you fans are still reeling over this season being the franchise's last in Connecticut. Over in Los Angeles, Sparks fans welcomed Caitlin Clark back to Crypto.com Arena for the first time since May of her rookie season, where she won her first-ever WNBA game.

items.headline: Olivia Miles' wild inbound pass
items.blurb: Olivia Miles has already made history in a Lynx uniform. After finishing with 15 points and six assists against the Wings, she joined Sue Bird and Candace Parker as the only players in WNBA history with at least 10 points and five assists in each of their first three career games. In a game full of breathtaking dimes, Miles' best may have been on a sideline out-of-bounds play in the fourth quarter. Lynx guard Kayla McBride came off a screen set by forward Natasha Howard at the top of the key, putting Wings guard Azzi Fudd on her back. From the right sideline, Miles perfectly timed and placed the pass to McBride under the basket and she was fouled from behind by Fudd.

longform.title: Why I don’t buy masculinism
longform.thesis: Masculinism — the organized ideological movement seeking to reverse women's legal and professional gains — is not a legitimate response to male struggles but a misogynist political project that has become the primary cohesive force on the American right.
longform.context: The piece serves as an author's note introducing Lewis's June 2026 Atlantic cover story, written amid the visible mainstreaming of anti-feminist ideology within the American right, including figures with direct proximity to the Trump administration such as Pete Hegseth.
arguments: Masculinism is a coherent political movement with named proponents and concrete policy goals — repealing the Nineteenth Amendment, instituting a 'family wage,' and reversing the 'great feminization' of professional life — not merely a cultural backlash or fringe internet phenomenon.

The movement's ideological toolkit conflates pseudoscience and grievance: figures like Raw Egg Nationalist argue that 'low testosterone causes liberalism,' while pastor Douglas Wilson claims 'feminism has made women ugly and unhappy,' framing policy goals as matters of biology and natural order rather than preference.

Lewis distinguishes between legitimate, underreported male struggles — citing research on male problem gambling — and the masculinists' broader claim that 'feminism has ruined America,' rejecting the latter as unsupported and politically motivated rather than evidence-based.

The masculinists' targeting of empathy as 'a dangerous, feminine softness toward immigrants and criminals' reveals that the movement's scope extends beyond gender politics into a broader authoritarian worldview, making it, in Lewis's framing, 'the single most important force holding together the American right.'
longform.significance: The piece matters because it documents the institutionalization of anti-feminist ideology within mainstream American conservatism at a moment of significant political power consolidation on the right. By naming specific figures and their policy proposals, Lewis moves the analysis beyond vague culture-war framing and identifies a concrete legislative and social agenda. The article implicitly argues that dismissing masculinism as fringe or absurd is a strategic error.
questions_raised: Lewis acknowledges that 'some men and boys are struggling in ways that don't get enough attention' but does not resolve how a serious policy response to male disadvantage can be disentangled from the masculinist framework that has captured that discourse.

The piece asserts masculinism is 'the single most important force holding together the American right' but leaves open whether that coalition is durable or whether the movement's more extreme proposals — like repealing the Nineteenth Amendment — represent genuine policy ambitions or rhetorical provocation.
